title: CHAPTER 3: Debut (1888 to 1891)

facts.fact: Irène's coming-out was engineered as an image: after a line in the society pages and a carefully staged photograph, the family summoned the Vianelli brothers from Venice—photographers to monarchs and the elite, able to make young women look like princesses of haute finance—so that the transformation could begin in the 'currency of daughters, dowries, arranged marriages, and wives-in-waiting'; the resulting portrait shows her at seventeen or eighteen in a gothic studded throne, corseted too tight, ribboned shoes on a damask pillow, face tilted away from the camera unsmiling as in her Renoir portrait.
facts.quote: A line in the society pages. A photograph of Irène, carefully staged. The Vianelli brothers were summoned from Venice, professional photographers to European monarchs and the elite. And they could make young women look like princesses of haute finance. This was how the transformation began in the currency of daughters, dowries, arranged marriages, and wives-in-waiting.

facts.fact: In the early spring of 1888, when Irène was still fifteen and everything was a rehearsal for marriage, the social season began unfolding at the family's hôtel particulier on rue Bassano: in April the Countess Cahen d'Anvers (Irène's mother Louise) hosted a comedy play in the drawing room that seemed to foretell Irène's future, recruiting Comédie-Française star Émilie Reichenberg from the invitation-only Cercle des Mirlitons, and Louise then staged her own grand salon for the one-act play La DeMoïselle à Marier, whose plot of a 'first interview' between a girl and a prospective groom was an audition-and-inspection comedy of manners.
facts.quote: That counted for something in the early spring of 1888, when she was still fifteen, when everything was a rehearsal for marriage. The social season had begun to unfold at her family’s vast hôtel particulier on rue Bassano. In April, the Countess Cahen d’Anvers hosted a comedy play in the drawing room that seemed to foretell Irène’s future. For the lead role, she recruited Émilie Reichenberg, a Comédie-Française star, who was performing at Le Cercle des Mirlitons, a private club on rue Royale where entry was by invitation only for the haute bourgeois.

facts.fact: The precedent for Irène's own arranging: around 1868 her father Louis and uncle Raphaël, thirty-one and twenty-seven respectively, travelled east to Trieste to meet two potential partners at the palatial home of the Morpurgo family, another Jewish banking dynasty, and had their 'first interview' with the sisters Louise (twenty-three) and Irène (nineteen), daughters of baron and private banker Giuseppe Morpurgo; Louis settled on Louise although everyone knew he had wanted the younger sister, second-choice Louise rebelled and turned yellow with stress-jaundice, was made to watch live fish so the illness could pass into another creature, and married Louis on June 30, 1868, her sister's alliance following on October 6.
facts.quote: Around 1868, Irène’s own father, Louis, and his brother, Raphaël—thirty-one and twenty-seven, respectively—had traveled east to Trieste, Italy, to meet two potential partners. Their destination: the palatial home of the Morpurgo family, another Jewish banking dynasty with aristocratic respectability. There, they had their first interview with the sisters Louise and Irène—the daughters of the baron and private banker Giuseppe Morpurgo. Louise was twenty-three. Irène, nineteen.

facts.fact: When it came to the next generation, Louise and Louis Cahen d'Anvers worked on marriage prospects for Irène first, not for their older son Robert, who would not marry until 1898: sons were allowed time to study, start a business in South America or vanish into an Argentine ranch, a son's missteps counted as 'experiences' while a daughter's delay was failure, because dowries were most appealing when the bride was young and newly visible—and so Irène lived for the season of balls in 1889 that marked her as eligible, dancing from midnight until 4:00 a.m. and giving, that March, a Sunday costume ball with forty place settings for intimate conversations in powdered wigs and ostrich feathers.
facts.quote: At the beginning, before everything that would follow, Irène lived for the season of balls in 1889 that marked her as eligible. Once the music began at midnight, she danced until 4:00 a.m. beneath the chandeliers, her laughter rising into the marble and gold. That March, there was a costume ball on Sunday with forty place settings arranged on small tables for intimate conversations.

facts.fact: In April, when Irène was nearly seventeen, Louise gave a grander ball and cotillion that the newspapers recorded as they were meant to be, L'Événement describing Irène as 'reigning' over a bataille de fleurs—the flower-throwing being choreographed matchmaking in which women flung blossoms toward admirers and suitors returned volleys, a lilac caught midair possibly beginning a relationship—while Raoul Montefiore, who also suffered the pressure, wrote that mothers stationed themselves near exits, that his parents lectured him into attending, and that his own family's ball cost 10,000 francs (something like $68,000 now).
facts.quote: In April, when Irène was nearly seventeen, Louise gave a grander ball and cotillion. The newspapers recorded it, just as they were meant to. L’Événement described Irène as if she were a sovereign—“reigning” over a bataille de fleurs of dancing. By two in the morning, they reported, Irène and her friends were scattering torn petals through the grand salon, their scent crushing into the parquet.

facts.fact: The Russian flu, arriving in Paris in December 1889 and blamed for more than a million deaths worldwide and sixty thousand in France, made the winter of 1890—the winter in which almost-eighteen Irène was in the right season for the machinery to move—a bad one; but by May 1890 the grippe had begun to fade and at the Hôtel Cahen d'Anvers they danced from midnight to four in the morning to celebrate Irène's debut as if none of it had happened, Irène in a pink froth of tulle, standing beside her mother to greet guests through l'entrée, where a liveried valet relayed calling cards and social rank dictated the order of entrance in her most public moment before a room full of potential husbands, mothers-in-law and rivals.
facts.quote: By May 1890, the grippe had begun to fade. And at the Hôtel Cahen d’Anvers, they danced to celebrate Irène’s debut. From midnight to four in the morning, they waltzed as if none of it had happened: the red blotches, the high fevers, the hallucinations, the complications of pneumonia.

facts.fact: By December 1890 Irène was skating with her younger sisters in ovals and deliberate loops at the Cercle de Patineurs in the Bois de Boulogne under the eyes of her watchful mother and governesses—skating being a frostbound ballroom where families timed visits to meet eligible young men and a girl 'seen' on the ice signaled eligibility, the New York Herald calling the Cahen d'Anvers sisters among the 'Rosy Beauties on the Ice'—and among the men warming their hands by the braziers towered an eligible bachelor already well known to her parents, Count Moïse de Camondo, the tall, monocled, one-eyed heir of the 'Rothschilds of the East'; eight months after those choreographed encounters on the frozen lake they were officially engaged, she eighteen, he thirty, and no one said the word 'love'.
facts.quote: While Irène and her sisters glided to the music, men warmed their hands by flaming braziers from the snowy banks. Among them—coincidentally or not—towered an eligible bachelor well known to Irène’s parents: Count Moïse de Camondo.

facts.fact: The match went public and then wobbled, before being sealed: Raoul Montefiore noticed how Irène changed and pulled away; several papers announced the engagement in the spring of 1891, but on May 10, 1891 La Liberté's announcement was contradicted ten days later by Le Figaro and others and by the New York Herald; by early August Le Figaro confirmed the engagement would be celebrated that Sunday at the Château de Beaulieu near Tours with the wedding to take place in Paris on October 20—a date that would change again—so in August 1891 the engagement was toasted at Beaulieu, where guests noted that the twelve-year age difference and Moïse's greater conservatism did not matter, and that Irène, still more girl than wife, had already begun a private battle against convention.
facts.quote: By early August, Le Figaro issued an update on Irène’s shaky engagement. “The marriage of Count Camondo and Mlle. Irène Cahen d’Anvers, daughter of Mr. Louis Cahen, which has been announced and then denied in turn, is now confirmed. The engagement will be celebrated today, Sunday, at the Château de Beaulieu (near Tours), where the Cahen family is currently staying. The wedding will take place in Paris on October 20.”

relationships: Irène Cahen d'Anvers (15-18 in this chapter) — daughter of Louis and Louise Cahen d'Anvers; the debutante whose society image, balls, skating and engagement are staged around her.

Louis Cahen d'Anvers (father) & Louise Cahen d'Anvers, the Countess (mother) — a marriage of transaction themselves (Trieste 1868, Louis took the 'second-choice' Louise though he had wanted her younger sister); they ran Irène's season, hosted the 1888 drawing-room comedy and grand-salon play, gave the 1889-1891 balls, and managed her match; Louise stood beside Irène at l'entrée and watched her on the ice.
Robert — the older brother whose marriage came last (not until 1898), illustrating that a son's delay was tolerated while a daughter's was failure.

Irène Morpurgo & Louise Morpurgo — the Morpurgo sisters of Trieste whom Louis and Raphaël went to interview; Louise married Louis on June 30, 1868 (Irène is thus Louise's younger sister and Irène Cahen d'Anvers's namesake aunt).
Raphaël — Louis's brother, companion on the Trieste trip (ages thirty-one and twenty-seven respectively).

Raoul Montefiore — Irène's cousin and neighbour, her closest friend until the day she got engaged; the source quoted on mothers guarding exits, ball costs (10,000 francs), and on walking home at daybreak with Gaston Arman de Caillavet and Proust; he noticed Irène changing and pulling away.

Count Moïse de Camondo ('Momo', 'One-eyed', 'Passy-Bourse') — tall, monocled, one-eyed (hunting accident) banker, last son of a Sephardic line from 1492 Spain, 'Rothschilds of the East'; after a year of unbroken mourning for Nissim (January 1889) and Abraham (mid-December 1889), and cousin Anselme Halphen's suicide, he ran Banque J. Camondo & Cie with Isaac de Camondo; he was well known to Irène's parents, courted her through the 1890 skating season and became her fiancé at thirty (she eighteen).

Nissim de Camondo (Moïse's father, died 1889 at fifty-eight) — had carried on a long, visible affair with Alice De Lancey, the Baltimore heiress who lived in du Barry's old pavilion at Louveciennes, parallel to the whispers about Louise's affair with the art critic Charles Ephrussi.
Émilie Reichenberg — Comédie-Française star recruited by the Countess for the April 1888 drawing-room comedy.
Marcel Proust — quoted on marriage as 'a social operation'; among the young men walking home at daybreak after balls with Raoul.

Thorstein Veblen & Célestine de Ségur — authorities invoked on conspicuous leisure and the winter season of marriage arranging; the New York Herald, L'Événement, Le Figaro, La Liberté, L'Illustration and the London Telegraph are the press that recorded and then corrected Irène's debut and engagement.

Raphaëla Cahen d'Anvers — Irène's younger cousin (her family had converted to Catholicism) who at eighteen married Prince Ferdinand de Faucigny-Lucinge, showing money outranking Catholic lineage after the 1882 Union Générale crash; Irène watched in pale rose silk and contemplated her own future.
Gaston Arman de Caillavet — with Proust, one of the young men Raoul walked home with at daybreak.
